question: How long must an authorised representative keep the technical paperwork for a general-purpose AI?
standalone_question: How long must an authorised representative keep the technical paperwork for a general-purpose AI?
answer:
An authorised representative (a person or company in the EU acting on behalf of an AI provider) must keep the technical paperwork for a period of 10 years after the general-purpose AI model is sold or placed on the market [Art. 3(5)], [Art. 54(3)(b)].

Key details include:
* The representative must keep a copy of the specific technical documentation described in Annex XI available for the AI Office and national authorities [Art. 54(3)(b)].
* The representative must also keep the contact details of the provider that appointed them for the same 10-year period [Art. 54(3)(b)].
* Upon receiving a reasoned request, they must provide this paperwork to the AI Office to prove compliance [Art. 54(3)(c)].

question: Under Article 8(2), if my product includes a high-risk AI system and is covered by other EU product laws, can I combine the required paperwork and testing?
standalone_question: Under Article 8(2) of the EU AI Act, if my product includes a high-risk AI system and is covered by other EU product laws, can I combine the required paperwork and testing?
answer:
Yes, you have the choice to combine your paperwork and testing [Art. 8(2)]. 

Here are the key details on how you can integrate them:
* Providers—the entities developing or offering the system—can integrate testing and reporting processes, information, and documentation into the existing procedures required by the EU product laws listed in Section A of Annex I [Art. 8(2)].
* This option is designed to ensure consistency, avoid duplicate efforts, and reduce extra burdens [Art. 8(2)].
* However, providers remain responsible for making sure the product fully complies with all applicable requirements across those EU product laws [Art. 8(2)].

This information is for guidance based on the Act's criteria and is not legal advice.

Where a product contains an AI system, to which the requirements of this Regulation as well as requirements of the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I apply, providers shall be responsible for ensuring that their product is fully compliant with all applicable requirements under applicable Union harmonisation legislation. In ensuring the compliance of high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1 with the requirements set out in this Section, and in order to ensure consistency, avoid duplication and minimise additional burdens, providers shall have a choice of integrating, as appropriate, the necessary testing and reporting processes, information and documentation they provide with regard to their product into documentation and procedures that already exist and are required under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I.

question: Can a high-risk AI be sold or used before its conformity checks are finished?
standalone_question: Can a high-risk AI system be sold or used before its conformity assessment procedures are completed under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Yes, a high-risk AI system (an AI system presenting significant health, safety, or fundamental rights risks) can be sold or used before completing standard conformity checks in specific exceptional cases [Art. 46(1)], [Art. 46(2)]. 

* A national market surveillance authority may grant permission to sell or use a specific system for a limited time while the required checks are finished without undue delay [Art. 46(1)].
* This temporary permission requires a justified request for exceptional reasons, such as public security, protecting human life and health, protecting the environment, or protecting vital industrial and infrastructure assets [Art. 46(1)].
* Law enforcement or civil protection authorities may start using a system immediately without prior approval in urgent situations involving exceptional public security reasons or specific, imminent threats to human life or physical safety [Art. 46(2)].
* In those urgent situations, the authorities must request authorisation without undue delay during or after use; if denied, use must stop at once and all results must be discarded immediately [Art. 46(2)].

By way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, any market surveillance authority may authorise the placing on the market or the putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems within the territory of the Member State concerned, for exceptional reasons of public security or the protection of life and health of persons, environmental protection or the protection of key industrial and infrastructural assets. That authorisation shall be for a limited period while the necessary conformity assessment procedures are being carried out, taking into account the exceptional reasons justifying the derogation. The completion of those procedures shall be undertaken without undue delay.

This is only allowed for exceptional reasons, such as public security, protecting people's life and health, environmental protection, or protecting key industrial and infrastructural assets. The required conformity assessment procedures must still be completed without undue delay.

question: How long do EU countries or the Commission have to object to a temporary measure taken against a risky AI system before it is considered justified?
standalone_question: How long do EU countries or the Commission have to object to a temporary measure taken against a risky AI system before it is considered justified under the EU AI Act?
answer:
A national temporary measure against a risky AI system is considered justified if no EU country or the Commission objects within three months of receiving notification [Art. 79(8)]. However, this deadline is shortened to 30 days if the issue involves prohibited AI practices [Art. 79(8)].

Key points to know:
* Standard deadline: EU countries and the Commission normally have three months from receiving the notification to raise an objection [Art. 79(8)].
* Prohibited practices: The objection period is reduced to 30 days if the system fails to comply with the ban on prohibited AI practices under Article 5 [Art. 79(8)].
* Effect of silence: If no one objects within the applicable time, the national measure is deemed justified [Art. 79(8)].
* Operators' rights: This time limit does not affect the procedural rights of the business operator under EU market surveillance rules [Art. 79(8)].

Where, within three months of receipt of the notification referred to in paragraph 5 of this Article, no objection has been raised by either a market surveillance authority of a Member State or by the Commission in respect of a provisional measure taken by a market surveillance authority of another Member State, that measure shall be deemed justified. This shall be without prejudice to the procedural rights of the concerned operator in accordance with Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. The three-month period referred to in this paragraph shall be reduced to 30 days in the event of non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 of this Regulation.

This timeframe is shortened to 30 days if the case involves non-compliance with prohibited AI practices.

question: Under Article 60(4)(h), what do providers need to do when they team up with deployers for real-world testing?
standalone_question: Under Article 60(4)(h) of the EU AI Act, what do providers need to do when they team up with deployers for real-world testing?
answer:
When a provider teams up with a deployer (a user of an AI system) to test in real-world conditions, they must share specific information and sign a formal agreement [Art. 60(4)(h)]. 

Specifically, they must meet the following rules:

* Inform the deployers about all details of the testing that could affect their choice to take part [Art. 60(4)(h)].
* Provide the deployers with the relevant instructions for using the AI system [Art. 60(4)(h)].
* Sign an agreement together that clearly defines each party's roles and responsibilities [Art. 60(4)(h)].
* Use that agreement to ensure both sides follow the rules for real-world testing under this Regulation as well as other EU and national laws [Art. 60(4)(h)].

question: Before asking a general-purpose AI provider to take action, can the AI Office talk to them first?
standalone_question: Before asking a general-purpose AI provider to take action, can the AI Office talk to them first under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Yes, the AI Office may start a structured dialogue with a provider—the entity that develops or provides a general-purpose AI model—before formally requiring actions or information [Art. 93(2)], [Art. 91(2)], [Art. 92(7)].

* The AI Office can begin a structured dialogue before requesting that a provider take measures [Art. 93(2)].
* During this dialogue, if a provider of a model with systemic risk offers commitments to address those risks, the Commission can make those commitments binding and end further action [Art. 93(3)].
* The AI Office can also start a structured dialogue before asking for documentation and information [Art. 91(2)].
* Before asking for access to evaluate a model, the AI Office may hold a structured dialogue to learn about internal testing, safeguards, and risk-mitigation measures [Art. 92(7)].

question: When I register a high-risk AI tool, do I need to include user instructions and a link for more info?
standalone_question: When registering a high-risk AI tool under the EU AI Act, do I need to include user instructions and a link for more info?
answer:
Yes, you must submit electronic instructions for use when registering a high-risk AI tool, unless an exception applies, while providing a web link is optional [Annex VIII, Section A, points 12–13]. 

* You must provide electronic instructions for use, but not if the high-risk AI tool is used in law enforcement, migration, asylum, or border control management [Annex VIII, Section A, points 12–13].
* Providing a URL for additional information is optional [Annex VIII, Section A, points 12–13].
* High-risk AI systems must generally include clear instructions for deployers (the people or entities using the tool) in an appropriate digital format or otherwise [Art. 13(2)].
* These instructions must cover details such as provider contact info, human oversight measures, and log-handling mechanisms where relevant [Art. 13(3)(a)], [Art. 13(3)(d)], [Art. 13(3)(f)].

question: If my company already has a monitoring plan under other EU laws, can we just add the AI Act requirements to it instead of making a new one?
standalone_question: If my company already has a monitoring plan under other EU laws, can we just add the AI Act requirements to it instead of making a new one?
answer:
Yes, you can integrate the required AI Act elements into an existing monitoring plan if your system qualifies under specific EU laws [Art. 72(4)]. 

* This option applies to high-risk AI systems (systems presenting significant risks to health, safety, or rights) covered by the EU laws listed in Section A of Annex I, or certain high-risk systems under Annex III point 5 sold or used by financial institutions [Art. 72(4)].
* To avoid duplicated work, providers (those who develop or supply the system) can incorporate the necessary AI post-market monitoring elements and template into their existing plans [Art. 72(4)].
* You can only do this if the combined setup achieves an equivalent level of protection [Art. 72(4)].
* The system must still actively collect and analyse performance data throughout its lifetime to ensure ongoing compliance [Art. 72(2)].

question: Under Article 93(3), what can the Commission do if a general-purpose AI provider promises to fix a systemic risk during talks?
standalone_question: Under Article 93(3) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, what can the Commission do if a general-purpose AI provider promises to fix a systemic risk during talks?
answer:
If a provider of a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk offers commitments to address a systemic risk at Union level during structured talks, the Commission can accept and enforce those promises [Art. 93(3)]. 

Specifically, the Commission may:
* Adopt a decision to make the provider's commitments binding [Art. 93(3)].
* Declare by decision that there are no further grounds for action [Art. 93(3)].

question: What authorities does each EU country have to set up to enforce the AI Act?
standalone_question: What national competent authorities do EU countries have to set up to enforce the AI Act?
answer:
Under the AI Act, EU countries must establish or designate notifying authorities and market surveillance authorities as their national competent authorities [Art. 3(48)], [Art. 70(2)]. 

* EU countries must designate one of their market surveillance authorities to serve as a single point of contact and inform the Commission of this choice [Art. 70(2)].
* Countries must tell the Commission who their notifying and market surveillance authorities are, explain their tasks, and publish electronic contact details by 2 August 2025 [Art. 70(2)].
* Countries must provide these authorities with adequate staff, funding, infrastructure, and technical expertise, reviewing these resources every year [Art. 70(3)].
* For AI systems used by European Union institutions, agencies, or bodies, the European Data Protection Supervisor acts as the national competent authority [Art. 3(48)].

Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.

Each Member State shall establish or designate as national competent authorities at least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority for the purposes of this Regulation. Those national competent authorities shall exercise their powers independently, impartially and without bias so as to safeguard the objectivity of their activities and tasks, and to ensure the application and implementation of this Regulation. The members of those authorities shall refrain from any action incompatible with their duties. Provided that those principles are observed, such activities and tasks may be performed by one or more designated authorities, in accordance with the organisational needs of the Member State.

These authorities must exercise their powers independently, impartially, and without bias, and their tasks may be performed by one or more designated authorities depending on the country's organisational needs.

question: Who else can get involved in AI regulatory sandboxes to help businesses and governments cooperate?
standalone_question: Who else can get involved in AI regulatory sandboxes to help businesses and governments cooperate?
answer:
National authorities running AI regulatory sandboxes can involve a wide range of public and private partners to encourage cooperation [Art. 57(4)], [Art. 58(2)(f)]. 

Key actors who can participate include:
* Innovators, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), start-ups, other businesses, and individual researchers [Art. 58(2)(f)].
* Testing and experimentation facilities, research labs, European Digital Innovation Hubs, and centres of excellence [Art. 58(2)(f)].
* Notified bodies (independent testing organisations that assess product conformity) and standardisation organisations [Art. 58(2)(f)].
* Deployers (users of AI systems) and other third parties who may partner with providers when submitting applications [Art. 58(2)(b)].

Additionally, national data protection authorities and other authorities supervising data access must be involved when the AI systems process personal data or fall under their oversight [Art. 57(10)].

question: Can EU countries ask the scientific panel's experts for help with enforcing the AI rules?
standalone_question: Can EU countries ask the scientific panel's experts for help with enforcing the AI rules under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act?
answer:
Yes, EU Member States can ask experts from the scientific panel to support their enforcement activities under the AI Act [Art. 69(1)].

Here are the key details on how this support works:

* Member States may specifically call upon the scientific panel's experts to support enforcement activities under the Regulation [Art. 69(1)].
* The panel also supports the work of national market surveillance authorities at their request, as well as cross-border market surveillance activities [Art. 68(3)(b)], [Art. 68(3)(c)].
* Panel experts must have up-to-date scientific or technical AI expertise, act independently from AI providers, and perform tasks objectively and without taking outside instructions [Art. 68(2)], [Art. 68(4)].
* The panel's general role is established to support enforcement activities across the EU [Art. 68(1)].

question: Can the EU ask general-purpose AI model makers for information if scientists need it for their work?
standalone_question: Can the EU ask general-purpose AI model makers for information if scientists need it for their work under the AI Act?
answer:
Yes, the European Commission can ask a general-purpose AI model maker for information to help scientists do their work [Art. 91(3)].

* The scientific panel must first make a well-supported request to the Commission [Art. 91(3)].
* The requested access to information must be both necessary and proportionate for the scientific panel to carry out its tasks under Article 68(2) [Art. 91(3)].
* The maker of the model, or its representative, is required to supply the requested information [Art. 91(5)].
* Authorized lawyers may supply this information for their clients, but the client remains fully responsible if the information is incomplete, incorrect, or misleading [Art. 91(5)].

question: Can providers of high-risk AI systems check their own compliance without using an external organization?
standalone_question: Can providers of high-risk AI systems perform conformity assessments internally without using a notified body or external organization under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Yes, providers of high-risk AI systems (the entities that develop or supply them) can perform conformity assessments internally without using a notified body in several situations [Art. 43(1)], [Art. 43(2)], [Art. 43(3)]. 

Here is how the rules apply:

* For high-risk AI systems listed in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, providers must follow an internal control procedure that does not involve a notified body [Art. 43(2)].
* For systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, providers can choose an internal control procedure if they have applied the relevant harmonised standards or common specifications [Art. 43(1)].
* However, for point 1 systems, providers must involve an external notified body if those standards or specifications do not exist, were not fully applied, or have published restrictions [Art. 43(1)].
* For systems covered by EU laws listed in Annex I, Section A, a manufacturer may opt out of third-party assessment only if the underlying law permits it and the manufacturer has applied all relevant harmonised standards or common specifications [Art. 43(3)].

question: Can the Commission bring in outside experts to help evaluate general-purpose AI models?

answer:

question: What does the Commission have to do when a new European technical standard is officially published?
standalone_question: What does the Commission have to do when a new European technical standard is officially published under the EU AI Act?
answer:
When an official reference to a harmonised standard is published in the Official Journal of the European Union, the Commission must repeal existing common specifications that cover the same ground [Art. 41(4)]. 

Key details include:
* First, when a European standardisation body proposes an adopted standard, the Commission must assess it under Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 [Art. 41(4)].
* Once the reference to that harmonised standard is published in the Official Journal, the Commission must repeal the implementing acts that established common specifications, or the parts of them covering the same high-risk requirements or general-purpose AI obligations [Art. 41(4)].

question: Do I need to register my high-risk AI system in an EU database before I start selling or using it?
standalone_question: Do I need to register my high-risk AI system in an EU database before I start selling or using it?
answer:
Yes, if your system falls under the relevant rules, it must be registered in the EU database before you sell or use it [Art. 49(1)], [Art. 49(3)]. 

Here are the main criteria:
* If you are a provider (someone who develops or sells the system) of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, you or your authorised representative must register yourself and the system before selling or using it, unless it falls under point 2 of Annex III [Art. 49(1)].
* Even if you decide your Annex III system is not high-risk based on the rules, you still must register yourself and the system in the database before selling or using it [Art. 49(2)], [Art. 6(4)].

question: Can using personal data in an AI regulatory sandbox affect the people whose data is being used or their privacy rights?
standalone_question: Can using personal data in an AI regulatory sandbox affect the people whose data is being used or their privacy rights under the EU AI Act?
answer:
No, using personal data in an AI regulatory sandbox cannot lead to measures or decisions that affect those individuals, nor can it affect their data protection rights [Art. 59(1)(f)]. 

Here are the key safeguards required when using personal data in a sandbox:

* Processing must not lead to measures or decisions affecting the individuals (data subjects), nor affect their rights under EU data protection law [Art. 59(1)(f)].
* Effective monitoring must detect high risks to individuals' rights and freedoms, with response tools to quickly reduce those risks or stop processing if needed [Art. 59(1)(c)].
* Data must be kept in a separate, isolated, and protected environment controlled by the prospective provider (the person or entity developing the system), with access restricted to authorised personnel [Art. 59(1)(d)].
* Data created in the sandbox cannot be shared outside of it, and original data can only be shared under EU data protection rules [Art. 59(1)(e)].

question: When is an AI system considered to present a risk?
standalone_question: When is an AI system considered to present a risk under the EU AI Act?

Under the EU AI Act, an AI system is considered to present a risk when it qualifies as a product presenting a risk under EU market surveillance rules, specifically where it poses risks to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of persons [Art. 79(1)]. 

Key details from the provided text include:

* The system must present risks to human health, safety, or fundamental rights to fall under this definition for national enforcement procedures [Art. 79(1)].
* For high-risk AI systems, providers must manage risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights that arise from normal intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse [Art. 9(2)(a)], [Art. 9(2)(b)].
* A related concept is systemic risk, which applies to general-purpose AI models whose capabilities can cause major negative effects across the EU on health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or society [Art. 3(65)].

question: Who can cancel a delegation of power, and does it affect rules that are already in place?
standalone_question: Who can cancel a delegation of power under the EU AI Act, and does it affect rules that are already in place?
answer:
Either the European Parliament or the Council can revoke a delegation of power at any time, and doing so does not affect rules that are already in force [Art. 97(3)].

Here is what matters most:
* The European Parliament or the Council can decide at any time to put an end to the specified delegation of power granted to the Commission [Art. 97(3)].
* The revocation takes effect the day after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union, or at a later date named in the decision [Art. 97(3)].
* Canceling the delegation does not change or invalidate any delegated acts that are already in force [Art. 97(3)].
* Additionally, either institution can prevent the power from being automatically renewed by opposing its extension at least three months before a five-year period ends [Art. 97(2)]. Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.

A decision of revocation shall put an end to the delegation of power specified in that decision. question: Why do high-risk AI tools need to be tested?
standalone_question: Why do high-risk AI systems need to be tested under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act?
answer:
High-risk AI systems—meaning AI tools that pose significant risks to safety or fundamental rights—must be tested to find the best risk management solutions and to prove they work properly and safely before they are sold or used [Art. 9(6)], [Art. 9(8)], [Art. 3(32)]. 

Testing serves several key purposes under the Act:

* Identifying the most appropriate and targeted measures to manage risks [Art. 9(6)].
* Ensuring the system performs consistently for its intended purpose and complies with legal requirements [Art. 9(6)].
* Providing an independent check using testing data to confirm the system's expected performance [Art. 3(32)].
* Qualifying for a presumption of compliance with specific data requirements, if the system is tested on data reflecting its intended geographical, behavioural, contextual, or functional setting [Art. 42(1)].

question: What happens if an AI provider fails to prove its general-purpose model does not pose systemic risks?

answer:
If a provider fails to convince the Commission that its general-purpose AI model does not present systemic risks, the Commission will reject the provider's arguments [Art. 52(3)]. As a result, the model is officially classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk [Art. 52(3)].

This classification triggers several requirements:
* The provider (the entity that develops or provides the model) must evaluate the model using state-of-the-art tools and conduct adversarial testing [Art. 55(1)(a)].
* The provider must assess and mitigate systemic risks at the EU level [Art. 55(1)(b)].
* The provider must ensure adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure, and promptly report serious incidents to the AI Office and national authorities [Art. 55(1)(c), Art. 55(1)(d)].
* If systemic risk concerns arise, the Commission can demand mitigation measures, restrict sales, withdraw, or recall the model [Art. 93(1)(b), Art. 93(1)(c)].

question: How long do other EU countries or the Commission have to object to an AI authorisation before it is automatically accepted?

Other EU countries or the Commission have 15 calendar days to object to an exceptional authorisation issued by a national market surveillance authority [Art. 46(4)]. If no objections are raised in that time, the authorisation is officially deemed justified [Art. 46(4)].

* If no EU country or the Commission objects within 15 calendar days of receiving that information, the authorisation is deemed justified [Art. 46(4)].
* If an objection is raised or the Commission sees legal or compliance issues within those 15 calendar days, the Commission must consult the country and operators and decide if the authorisation is justified [Art. 46(5)].
* If the Commission decides the authorisation is not justified, the national authority must withdraw it [Art. 46(6)].

question: What is the maximum fine for an EU institution that uses banned AI practices?

* It enters into consultations without undue delay with the relevant Member States and operators [Art. 82(4)].

question: How are the members of the AI scientific panel chosen, and what qualifications do they need?

answer:
The European Commission selects the members of the scientific panel based on up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI [Art. 68(2)]. 

* Selection and size: The Commission chooses the experts, decides the total number needed in consultation with the European Artificial Intelligence Board, and must ensure a fair balance of gender and geographical representation [Art. 68(2)].
* Technical qualifications: Candidates must demonstrate particular expertise, competence, and up-to-date scientific or technical knowledge in AI needed to advise and support the AI Office [Art. 68(2)].
* Independence and objectivity: Panel members must be independent from any provider (the person or entity developing or branding the AI) of AI systems or general-purpose AI models, and they must be able to work diligently, accurately, and objectively [Art. 68(2)].
* Integrity rules: Once selected, experts must act impartially, protect confidential information, refuse instructions from anyone, and submit a publicly available declaration of interests [Art. 68(4)].

question: What happens if a serious risk is found while testing an AI system in a regulatory sandbox?

answer:

* Any significant risks identified to health, safety, or fundamental rights during development and testing must result in adequate mitigation [Art. 57(11)].
* Competent authorities supervising the sandbox retain their supervisory and corrective powers [Art. 57(11)].
* If effective mitigation is not possible, national authorities have the power to temporarily or permanently suspend the testing or the participant's involvement in the sandbox, and they must inform the AI Office [Art. 57(11)].
* If personal data is processed in the sandbox, response mechanisms must promptly mitigate any high risks to individuals' rights and freedoms and, if necessary, stop the data processing [Art. 59(1)(c)].

question: Do high-risk AI tools need to be supervised by people while they are being used?
standalone_question: Do high-risk AI tools need to be supervised by people while they are being used under the EU AI Act?
answer:

* This oversight aims to prevent or reduce risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights during normal use or reasonably foreseeable misuse [Art. 14(2)].
* Oversight can be built directly into the system by the provider (the maker) or set up as measures to be carried out by the deployer (the user) [Art. 14(3)].
* The people supervising the tool must be able to understand its abilities, watch for flaws, avoid blindly trusting it, correctly read its outputs, and ignore or reverse its decisions [Art. 14(4)(a)], [Art. 14(4)(b)], [Art. 14(4)(c)], [Art. 14(4)(d)].
* Overseers must also be able to step in or stop the system safely using a "stop" button or similar process [Art. 14(4)(e)], and deployers must ensure these people have the right training, skills, authority, and support [Art. 26(2)].

question: What rights does an EU agency have before the data protection supervisor fines it?

* The right to be heard regarding the possible infringement before any final decision is made [Art. 100(4)].
* The right to comment on all elements and circumstances, with the Supervisor allowed to base decisions only on facts the agency could comment on [Art. 100(4)].
* The guarantee that its rights of defence will be fully respected throughout the proceedings [Art. 100(5)].
* The right of access to the Supervisor's case file, limited only by the legitimate protection of other parties' personal data or business secrets [Art. 100(5)].

* Immediately take necessary corrective actions to make the system comply, or else disable, withdraw, or recall it [Art. 20(1)].
* Inform distributors, authorized representatives, importers, and users (deployers), as applicable [Art. 20(1)].
* If the system presents a risk under Article 79(1), immediately investigate the causes, working with the user who reported it if relevant [Art. 20(2)].
* If there is such a risk, notify the relevant market surveillance authorities and any certifying body involved, explaining the non-compliance and the corrective actions taken [Art. 20(2)].

* Alternatively, the high-risk AI system must be put into use under the manufacturer's name or trademark after the product has already been sold [Art. 25(3)(b)].

question: Can a notified body hire another company or use a subsidiary to do part of an AI assessment, and what must they do if they do?

question: If a company qualifies for a special innovation exemption, does it still have to follow the rest of the AI Act's rules?

answer:

Here is how the rules apply under these special measures:
* Microenterprises without partner or linked enterprises may follow certain quality management rules in a simplified way, but this cannot lower the level of protection or remove the need to comply with high-risk AI system requirements [Art. 63(1)].
* Participants in an AI regulatory sandbox remain liable under regular liability laws for any harm caused to third parties during their experiments [Art. 57(12)].
* Sandbox participation does not remove the supervisory or corrective powers of authorities, and testing can be suspended if significant risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights cannot be mitigated [Art. 57(11)].
* Testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions outside sandboxes still requires specific official approvals and registration in EU databases [Art. 60(4)(b)], [Art. 60(4)(c)].

question: What rules do authorities have to follow when they collect and handle data about AI systems?

answer:

Key rules include:
* Authorities may only request data strictly necessary to assess risks and carry out their legal powers, and they must delete it once it is no longer needed [Art. 78(2)].
* They must maintain confidentiality to protect business secrets, intellectual property (including source code), public security, classified information, and ongoing investigations or legal proceedings [Art. 78(1)].
* When dealing with certain sensitive high-risk AI systems used or provided by law enforcement, border control, or immigration authorities, confidential information cannot be shared without prior consultation, sensitive operational data must not be exchanged, and documentation access requires proper security clearance [Art. 78(3)].
* For AI regulatory testing sandboxes, national authorities must involve data protection authorities and other relevant regulators whenever innovative systems involve personal data or fall under those regulators' oversight [Art. 57(10)].

* Following these standards allows providers (entities developing or selling the system) to choose internal control procedures for certain systems, whereas failing to apply them in full may force the involvement of an external notified body [Art. 43(1)].
* Meeting recognized cybersecurity certification schemes similarly creates a presumption of compliance specifically for cybersecurity requirements [Art. 42(2)].
* If official standards do not cover all legal requirements, you must still fulfill the remaining rules through other means, such as common specifications [Art. 40(1)], [Art. 41(3)], [Art. 43(1)].

question: When is a general-purpose AI considered to have systemic risk?
standalone_question: When is a general-purpose AI considered to have systemic risk according to the EU Artificial Intelligence Act?
answer:
A general-purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities or if the European Commission decides it has an equivalent impact [Art. 51(1)]. Systemic risk refers to risks tied to these high-impact capabilities that can cause major harm across the EU market, society, public safety, or fundamental rights, spreading widely across the value chain [Art. 3(65)].

Key rules for this classification include:
- A model is automatically presumed to have high-impact capabilities if the total computing power used to train it exceeds 10^25 floating point operations [Art. 51(2)].
- A model qualifies if technical benchmarks show high-impact capabilities, or if the Commission decides on its own initiative or after an alert from a scientific panel that its impact is equivalent based on Annex XIII criteria [Art. 51(1)].
- When a model meets the high-impact capability condition, the provider (the person or entity developing the model) must notify the Commission within two weeks, though they can argue that specific characteristics prevent it from posing systemic risks [Art. 52(1)], [Art. 52(2)].

question: What information do authorities have to share when they report a risky or rule-breaking AI system?

Under the provided rules, authorities must share:

* When a compliant system presents a risk, Member States must immediately give the Commission and other Member States all available details, specifically data to identify the AI system, its origin and supply chain, the type of risk involved, and the nature and duration of national measures taken [Art. 82(3)].
* In procedures for AI systems presenting a risk, other market surveillance authorities must inform the Commission and other Member States without undue delay about any measures they adopted, extra information on the system's non-compliance, and any objections they have [Art. 79(7)].
* If an incorrectly classified non-high-risk system is used beyond national borders, authorities must promptly inform the Commission and other Member States of their evaluation results and the actions required of the provider (the entity offering the system) [Art. 80(3)].
* Authorities must also submit annual reports to the Commission covering the use of prohibited practices and measures taken [Art. 74(2)], as well as annual reports on authorized law enforcement use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in public spaces, including decision numbers and results [Art. 5(6)].

question: Are there any situations where the right to an explanation for an AI decision doesn't apply?

* It does not apply when exceptions or restrictions to this obligation exist under Union or national law that complies with Union law [Art. 86(2)], [Recital 171].
* It only applies if the right to an explanation is not already provided for under other Union law [Art. 86(3)], [Recital 171].
* The entire Act—including this right—does not apply to AI systems used exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes, or outside the scope of Union law [Art. 2(3)].

question: How can companies making general-purpose AI prove they follow the rules?

* They may follow approved codes of practice to show compliance until European harmonised standards are officially published [Art. 53(4)], [Art. 55(2)], [Recital 117].
* Meeting European harmonised standards gives these companies a presumption that they conform to the required rules, provided the standards cover those obligations [Art. 53(4)], [Art. 55(2)], [Recital 117].
* If they do not use an approved code of practice or a European harmonised standard, they must present alternative adequate means of compliance for the European Commission to assess [Art. 53(4)], [Art. 55(2)], [Recital 117].
* Providers must also supply requested information, technical documentation, and access to authorities to verify compliance, including records of their training, testing, and copyright policies [Art. 53(1)(a)], [Art. 91(5)], [Art. 92(5)], [Recital 164].

question: Does the EU look at power imbalances or vulnerability when deciding if an AI system is high-risk?

* When assessing whether to add systems to the high-risk list, the European Commission must evaluate if there is an imbalance of power or if people facing potential harm are in a vulnerable position compared to the deployer, which is the person or entity using the AI [Art. 7(2)(h)].
* This vulnerability can stem from status, authority, knowledge, age, or social and economic circumstances [Art. 7(2)(h)].
* The Commission must also look at whether the potential harm or adverse impact disproportionately affects a specific group of persons [Art. 7(2)(f)].
* Additionally, providers developing high-risk AI systems must consider whether the system is likely to negatively impact children under 18 or other vulnerable groups when managing risks [Art. 9(9)].

question: How are the rules set for the scientific panel to send out warnings or ask the AI Office for help?

The rules for the scientific panel to issue alerts and seek assistance are defined through an implementing act [Art. 68(5)]. 

Key details on how this works include:
* The implementing act sets out the specific conditions, procedures, and detailed arrangements for the panel and its members to issue alerts and request help from the AI Office [Art. 68(5)].
* The panel advises the AI Office by alerting it to possible systemic risks across the Union from general-purpose AI models [Art. 68(3)(a)(i)].

* A qualified alert must be reasoned and include the model provider's contact point, the facts and reasons for the alert, and any other relevant details gathered by the panel [Art. 90(3)].

question: If my AI model is classified as having systemic risk, how soon can I ask the Commission to review that decision?

You can ask the Commission to reassess the classification at the earliest six months after the designation decision [Art. 52(5)]. 

Here are the key rules for this request:
* A provider (the person or entity that develops the model) can make a reasoned request if their model was designated as presenting systemic risks by the Commission [Art. 52(4)], [Art. 52(5)].
* The request must include objective, detailed, and new reasons that have appeared since the initial decision [Art. 52(5)].
* If the Commission reassesses the model and decides to keep the systemic risk designation, you must wait at least another six months after that decision before requesting another review [Art. 52(5)].

question: Who can fine EU agencies if they break the AI rules, and what factors determine the amount?

The European Data Protection Supervisor can impose administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies that fall under the Regulation [Art. 100(1)]. 

When deciding whether to issue a fine and calculating its amount, the Supervisor must consider all relevant circumstances of the case, giving due regard to:

* The nature, gravity, and duration of the breach and its results, including the purpose of the artificial intelligence (AI) system, the number of people harmed, and how much damage they suffered [Art. 100(1)(a)].
* The agency's level of responsibility based on its technical and organisational measures, actions taken to lessen the damage to affected persons, and any similar past breaches [Art. 100(1)(b)], [Art. 100(1)(c)], [Art. 100(1)(e)].
* The agency's cooperation with the Supervisor to fix the problem and lessen its negative effects, including obeying previous orders regarding the same issue [Art. 100(1)(d)].

standalone_question: Can companies test high-risk AI in the real world without using a regulatory sandbox under the AI Act?
answer:
Yes, companies can test high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions outside of regulatory sandboxes, provided they meet specific legal requirements [Art. 60(1)]. A high-risk AI system is an AI system identified under the Act as carrying significant risks, such as those listed in Annex III [Art. 60(1)].

Here are the main rules that apply:

* Testing can be carried out by providers (those developing the system) alone or with deployers (those using it) at any time before selling or using the system [Art. 60(2)], without violating bans on prohibited AI practices [Art. 60(1)] or required ethical reviews [Art. 60(3)].
* The provider must prepare a testing plan and submit it to the national market surveillance authority [Art. 60(4)(a)], which must approve it; tacit approval applies after 30 days unless national law requires explicit authorization [Art. 60(4)(b)].
* The testing must be properly registered in the relevant EU database [Art. 60(4)(c)], and the predictions, recommendations, or decisions made by the AI system during the test must be able to be reversed and disregarded [Art. 60(4)(k)].
* Providers must notify the authority when the testing is paused, finished, and share the final results [Art. 60(8)].

question: How reliable and secure do high-risk AI systems have to be?
standalone_question: How reliable and secure do high-risk AI systems have to be under the EU AI Act?
answer:
High-risk AI systems—AI tools that pose significant risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights—must be designed to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and perform consistently throughout their entire lifecycle [Art. 15(1)]. Their design must reflect their intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art [Art. 8(1)].

Key requirements for reliability and security include:

* Systems must be as resilient as possible against errors, faults, or inconsistencies caused by interactions with people or other systems, using technical solutions like backup plans or redundancy [Art. 15(4)].
* Systems that continue learning after being sold or used must eliminate or minimize the risk of biased feedback loops [Art. 15(4)], and their accuracy levels and metrics must be stated in their instructions [Art. 15(3)].
* Systems must resist attacks by unauthorized third parties to alter their use, outputs, or performance, with specific protections against data poisoning, model poisoning, and adversarial inputs [Art. 15(5)].
* Providers—entities that develop such systems—must test systems before, during, and after development to manage risks and ensure consistent performance [Art. 9(6)], [Art. 17(1)(d)], [Art. 16(a)].

question: What basic details do companies building general-purpose AI have to put in their technical files?
standalone_question: What basic details do companies building general-purpose AI have to put in their technical files under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Providers (the entities that develop or build the AI) of general-purpose AI models must create and maintain technical documentation to provide to authorities upon request [Art. 53(1)(a)]. 

This documentation must contain at least the following basic details:

* A general overview of the model, covering its intended tasks, acceptable use policies, release date, distribution channels, architecture, parameter count, input/output formats and modalities, and its licence [Annex XI, Section 1, point 1].
* Technical integration details, including the necessary tools, infrastructure, and instructions to integrate the model into AI systems [Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(a)].
* Development and design specifications, explaining the training process, key design choices, what the model optimizes for, parameter relevance, and training computational resources and energy use [Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(b), (d), (e)].
* Information about the data used for training, testing, and validation, including data types, sources, curation methods, size, and measures taken to spot unsuitable data sources or biases [Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(c)].

question: What information about testing and security do I need to include in the technical documentation under Annex IV point 2?

* Information on validation and testing procedures, including the data used and their main characteristics [Annex IV, point 2].
* Metrics applied to measure accuracy, robustness, compliance with specific requirements, and any potentially discriminatory impacts [Annex IV, point 2].
* Test logs and all test reports that are dated and signed by the responsible persons, including those covering pre-determined changes to the system [Annex IV, point 2].
* The cybersecurity measures put in place for the AI system [Annex IV, point 2].

question: When can the European Commission remove conditions for high-risk AI systems?
standalone_question: When can the European Commission remove conditions for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act?
answer:

* The Commission must adopt delegated acts to delete any of the conditions set out in Article 6(3), second subparagraph [Art. 6(7)].
* There must be concrete and reliable evidence showing that the deletion is needed to maintain the level of protection for health, safety, and fundamental rights set by this Regulation [Art. 6(7)].
* Separately, the Commission may also remove high-risk AI systems entirely from the Annex III list if they no longer pose significant risks and the deletion does not lower the overall protection under Union law [Art. 7(3)].

question: How do notified bodies adapt their processes for different AI companies?
standalone_question: How do notified bodies adapt their processes for different AI companies under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Notified bodies must adapt their procedures by considering the specific characteristics of the company and the AI system, while avoiding unnecessary burdens [Art. 31(8)], [Art. 34(2)]. 

* Notified bodies must have procedures that take due account of a provider's size, structure, operating sector, and the complexity of the AI system [Art. 31(8)], [Art. 34(2)].
* They must avoid creating unnecessary burdens for providers, specifically aiming to reduce administrative burdens and compliance costs for micro- and small enterprises [Art. 34(2)]. A provider is an entity that develops an AI system and places it on the market or puts it into service.
* Despite adjusting for company size and system complexity, notified bodies must still maintain the required level of protection and strictness needed for the high-risk AI system to comply with the rules [Art. 34(2)].

question: How much time does a company have to fix or remove a non-compliant AI system if a regulator finds it poses a risk?
standalone_question: How much time does a company have to fix or remove a non-compliant AI system if a regulator finds it poses a risk under the EU AI Act?
answer:
If a market surveillance authority finds that an AI system presenting a risk does not comply with the rules, the company must take action within a period set by that authority [Art. 79(2)]. This period cannot exceed 15 working days, or a shorter timeframe if one is set by relevant Union harmonisation legislation [Art. 79(2)].

Key details include:

* The regulator can order the operator to fix the AI system, withdraw it from the market, or recall it [Art. 79(2)].
* The deadline is whatever period the regulator prescribes, but it must be within the shorter of 15 working days or the limit under relevant Union harmonisation legislation [Art. 79(2)].
* Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.

* They must share information about quality system approvals and technical documentation assessment certificates (or supplements) that they have issued, but only upon request [Art. 45(2)(a)], [Art. 45(2)(b)].

question: How does the AI Board help different countries' authorities work together?

* It brings together one representative from each EU member state who is empowered to coordinate national authorities and serve as a single point of contact [Art. 65(2)], [Art. 65(4)(b)], [Art. 65(4)(c)].
* It sets up two standing sub-groups to provide cooperation and exchange platforms specifically for market surveillance authorities and for notifying authorities, and can create additional sub-groups for specific issues [Art. 65(6)].
* It helps the AI Office support national authorities in setting up AI regulatory sandboxes (controlled testing environments) and facilitates cooperation and sharing information between those sandboxes [Art. 66(k)].
* It allows other national authorities and experts to be invited to meetings on a case-by-case basis whenever relevant topics are discussed [Art. 65(2)].

question: Do the rules for AI supply chains still protect company secrets and patents?

Yes, the EU AI Act includes specific rules to protect intellectual property rights, confidential business information, and trade secrets across the AI supply chain [Art. 25(5)], [Recital 88].

Here is what matters most:

* Value chain responsibilities regarding high-risk AI systems—systems that create significant risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights—must respect and protect intellectual property rights, confidential business information, and trade secrets under EU and national law [Art. 25(5)].
* Third parties who supply tools, services, or components must help high-risk AI providers (those who develop or sell AI systems) through written agreements, but they should do so without compromising their own intellectual property rights or trade secrets [Art. 25(4)], [Recital 88].
* Authorities and any other persons involved in applying the Act must respect confidentiality to protect trade secrets, confidential business information, and intellectual property, including source code, subject to limited exceptions under EU law [Art. 78(1)(a)].
* Information and trade secrets collected from providers of general-purpose AI models are strictly subject to these confidentiality rules [Art. 53(7)], [Art. 55(3)].

question: If I need to report a serious incident quickly, can I submit an unfinished report first?

* The standard deadline is immediately after finding a causal link or reasonable likelihood of one, and no later than 15 days after becoming aware of the incident [Art. 73(2)].
* Deadlines are shorter in severe cases: within two days for widespread infringements or disruptions to critical infrastructure, and within 10 days if a person dies [Art. 73(3)], [Art. 73(4)].

question: When can the scientific panel send a warning to the AI Office about an AI model?

answer:
The scientific panel can issue a warning, known as a qualified alert, to the AI Office whenever it suspects that a general-purpose AI model poses specific EU-wide risks or meets certain statutory conditions [Art. 90(1)]. This warning advises the AI Office on possible systemic risks across the EU [Art. 68(3)].

Specifically, the scientific panel may send an alert when it has reason to suspect that:
* The model poses a concrete, identifiable risk at the Union level [Art. 90(1)].
* The model meets the conditions set out in Article 51 [Art. 90(1)].
* The alert is properly justified and includes the contact point of the model's provider (the entity offering the model), relevant facts and reasons, and any extra information gathered by the panel [Art. 90(3)].

question: What powers do authorities have to check on real-world testing of high-risk AI?

High-risk AI systems are artificial intelligence tools that present significant risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights [Art. 60(1)].

The authorities hold the following powers to check and supervise testing:

* They can demand information from providers (those who develop or offer the AI system) and prospective providers [Art. 60(6)].
* They can perform checks on the test conduct and the AI systems, including carrying out unannounced remote or on-site inspections [Art. 60(6)].
* They have the authority to approve the real-world testing and the testing plan, which can occur tacitly if they do not reply within 30 days unless national law requires explicit authorisation [Art. 60(4)(b)].
* If an incident occurs or rules are breached, they can order the provider or deployer (the user of the system) to modify the testing, or they can suspend or terminate the test entirely [Art. 76(3)].

question: What happens if a notified body stops meeting its requirements or obligations?
standalone_question: What happens if a notified body stops meeting its requirements or obligations under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act?
answer:
If a notified body stops meeting its requirements or obligations, the relevant authority must investigate and restrict, suspend, or withdraw its official designation [Art. 36(4)]. The European Commission can also step in if the Member State fails to take action [Art. 37(4)].

* The notifying authority must promptly investigate, let the body share its views, and restrict, suspend, or withdraw the designation based on how serious the failure is, then immediately inform the Commission and other EU countries [Art. 36(4)].
* The Commission will investigate any doubts about the body's competence or compliance [Art. 37(1)] and request corrective steps from the Member State [Art. 37(4)].
* If the Member State does not act, the Commission can adopt an implementing act to directly suspend, restrict, or withdraw the designation [Art. 37(4)].
* Failing to meet requirements and obligations under Article 31 can lead to fines of up to 15 million euros or up to 3% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher [Art. 99(4)].

If the notifying authority comes to the conclusion that the notified body no longer meets the requirements laid down in Article 31 or that it is failing to fulfil its obligations, it shall restrict, suspend or withdraw the designation as appropriate, depending on the seriousness of the failure to meet those requirements or fulfil those obligations. * Member States must check and update resource and skill requirements on an annual basis to ensure authorities can perform their duties effectively [Art. 70(3)].
* Authorities must permanently have enough staff with expertise in AI technologies, data, cybersecurity, fundamental rights, safety risks, standards, and legal requirements [Art. 70(3)].
* Starting by 2 August 2025, and then every two years, Member States must report to the Commission on whether their authorities have adequate financial and human resources [Art. 70(6)]. Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.
* The Commission shares these reports with the Board for discussion and recommendations, and also reviews authority resources in its own evaluation reports [Art. 70(6)], [Art. 112(4)(a)].

question: Does the EU AI Act apply to companies outside Europe if their AI is used in the EU?

answer:

Here is what matters most:

* The rules apply to providers (those who develop AI systems or general-purpose models) sell or use them in the Union, even if the providers are established in a third country outside Europe [Art. 2(1)(a)].

* This rule prevents companies from avoiding the law by keeping the AI system outside Europe while sending its results back into the Union [Recital 22].
* However, the Act does not apply if the AI system or its output is used exclusively for military, defence, or national security purposes [Art. 2(3)].

question: What factors are used to decide if a general-purpose AI has a systemic risk?
standalone_question: What factors are used to decide if a general-purpose AI model has a systemic risk under the EU AI Act?
answer:
A general-purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities or if the European Commission decides it has equivalent capabilities or impact [Art. 51(1)]. 

The key factors used to decide this include:

* A model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities if the total computing power used to train it exceeds 10^25 floating point operations [Art. 51(2)].
* Evaluated technical capabilities, assessed using appropriate technical tools, benchmarks, indicators, input and output modalities, autonomy, adaptability, and access to tools [Art. 51(1)(a)], [Annex XIII, points (d), (e)].
* Training and design factors, including the number of parameters, the size or quality of the dataset, and the computation used for training (or related measures like training cost, time, or energy use) [Annex XIII, points (a), (b), (c)].
* Market reach and user numbers, including the number of registered end-users and whether it reaches at least 10,000 registered business users established in the Union [Annex XIII, points (f), (g)].

question: Who sets the penalties for breaking the AI rules, and what do they have to keep in mind for startups?

EU Member States set the rules on penalties and other enforcement measures for breaking the AI rules [Art. 99(1)].

* Member States must take into account the interests and economic viability of SMEs, including start-ups [Art. 99(1)].
* Penalties must always be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive [Art. 99(1)].
* For SMEs and start-ups, any fine must be capped at whichever is lower between the set fixed amount or the percentage of turnover [Art. 99(6)].
* When deciding whether to fine and calculating the amount, authorities must consider specific circumstances, including the operator's size, annual turnover, and market share [Art. 99(7)(d)].

question: If the police use an AI lie detector, is that considered a high-risk system?
standalone_question: If the police use an AI lie detector, is that considered a high-risk system under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Yes, an AI lie detector used by the police is considered a high-risk AI system under the EU AI Act, provided its use is permitted under relevant Union or national law [Annex III, point 6]. A high-risk AI system is a tool subject to strict legal requirements due to its significant potential impact on fundamental rights [Recital 59]. 

* Systems intended for use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities as polygraphs or similar tools are explicitly listed as high-risk [Annex III, point 6(b)].
* This classification applies as long as their use is legally permitted under Union or national law [Annex III, point 6].
* Similar polygraph tools used by public authorities in migration, asylum, and border control management are also classified as high-risk under permitted law [Annex III, point 7(a)].
* The Act classifies these tools as high-risk because law enforcement actions carry risks of power imbalance, arrest, deprivation of liberty, and impacts on fundamental rights like fair trial and defence rights [Recital 59].

* A copy of the written EU declaration of conformity, which states that the system meets regulatory standards [Art. 47(1)].

question: What does Article 50(1) require for AI that talks directly to people, and what are the exceptions?
standalone_question: What does Article 50(1) of the EU AI Act require for AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons, and what are the exceptions?
answer:
Providers (those who develop or have an AI system developed) must design and build systems meant to interact directly with people so that individuals are informed they are interacting with an AI system [Art. 50(1)]. This notice must be given in a clear and distinguishable way at the latest during the first interaction, following accessibility rules [Art. 50(5)].

* Providers do not need to give this notice if it is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant, and circumspect person, considering the context and circumstances [Art. 50(1)].
* The requirement does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences, provided appropriate safeguards protect third-party rights and freedoms [Art. 50(1)].
* However, the law enforcement exception does not apply if the AI system is made available for the public to report a criminal offence [Art. 50(1)].

* If the notification includes specific documentary evidence instead, the waiting period is two months without objection [Art. 30(4)].

question: When can the European Commission update the rules for AI systems that aren't actually high-risk?
standalone_question: When can the European Commission update the rules for AI systems that are not classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act?
answer:
The European Commission can update the conditions under which certain AI systems are not considered high-risk by adopting delegated acts [Art. 6(6)], [Art. 6(7)]. 

The Commission can make these updates in the following situations:

* It can add new conditions or modify existing ones when concrete and reliable evidence shows that certain systems fall under Annex III but do not pose a significant risk of harm to people's health, safety, or fundamental rights [Art. 6(6)].
* It must delete existing conditions when concrete and reliable evidence shows this is necessary to keep the level of protection for health, safety, and fundamental rights intact [Art. 6(7)].
* Additionally, the Commission must provide guidelines by 2 February 2026, after consulting the European Artificial Intelligence Board, specifying how to practically implement these rules along with practical examples of high-risk and non-high-risk use cases [Art. 6(5)]. Later amendments to the Act are not reflected in this text.

question: Are there quality rules for the data used to train high-risk AI?
standalone_question: Are there quality rules for the data used to train high-risk AI under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Yes, the EU AI Act sets specific quality rules for data used to train high-risk AI systems [Art. 10(1)]. When AI models are trained on data, the training, validation, and testing datasets must meet mandatory quality standards [Art. 10(1)].

What matters most includes:
* Datasets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and as free of errors and complete as possible for their intended purpose [Art. 10(3)].
* Datasets must have suitable statistical properties, including for the specific people or groups the system will be used on [Art. 10(3)].
* Datasets must account for specific geographical, contextual, behavioural, or functional settings where the system is meant to be used [Art. 10(4)].
* Providers (those who develop or sell the AI) must set up a documented quality management system that covers data management operations like collecting, labelling, filtering, and storing data [Art. 17(1)(f)].

reference_answer_generated: Yes, high-risk AI systems that train models with data must be developed using training, validation, and testing data sets that meet specific quality criteria whenever those data sets are used.
judge_reasons: No issues.

answer:
The Board helps national authorities and the Commission build required skills by assisting them in developing organizational and technical expertise to implement the rules [Art. 66(j)]. 

Key ways the Board provides this support under this provision include:
- Assisting national competent authorities and the Commission in developing necessary organizational and technical expertise [Art. 66(j)].
- Helping assess the specific training needs of staff in Member States who are involved in implementing the Regulation [Art. 66(j)].

question: Under Article 10(5), when can providers use sensitive personal data to fix bias in high-risk AI systems?
standalone_question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when can providers use sensitive personal data to fix bias in high-risk AI systems?
answer:
Providers—meaning those who develop or provide AI systems—may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only when it is strictly necessary to detect and correct bias in high-risk AI systems [Art. 10(5)].

To do so, they must follow EU data protection laws, provide safeguards for fundamental rights, and satisfy all of the following conditions [Art. 10(5)]:

* Bias detection and correction cannot be effectively achieved using other data, including synthetic or anonymised data [Art. 10(5)(a)].
* The data is protected by technical limits on re-use, state-of-the-art security, privacy-preserving measures like pseudonymisation, and strict access controls ensuring only authorised personnel under confidentiality obligations have access [Art. 10(5)(b)], [Art. 10(5)(c)].
* The data cannot be transmitted, transferred, or accessed by other parties [Art. 10(5)(d)].
* The data is deleted as soon as the bias is corrected or its retention period ends, and the provider records the reasons showing why using this data was strictly necessary instead of other data [Art. 10(5)(e)], [Art. 10(5)(f)].
reference_answer_generated: Under Article 10(5), providers of high-risk AI systems can exceptionally process special categories of personal data if it is strictly necessary for bias detection and correction and cannot be achieved using other data like synthetic or anonymised data. They must apply strict safeguards, including technical limitations on reuse, pseudonymisation, access controls, and a ban on sharing the data with other parties. The data must also be deleted once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, and the reasons for using it must be documented.

question: Do authorised representatives have to work with authorities to lower the risks of a high-risk AI?
standalone_question: Do authorised representatives have to work with authorities to lower the risks of a high-risk AI?
answer:
Yes, an authorised representative must cooperate with authorities to lower and mitigate the risks posed by a high-risk AI system [Art. 22(3)(d)]. 

Here are the key requirements regarding this duty:

* The written mandate from the provider—the entity supplying the AI—must empower the representative to cooperate with competent authorities upon a reasoned request [Art. 22(1)], [Art. 22(3)(d)].
* This cooperation specifically includes any action the authorities take to reduce and mitigate the risks posed by the high-risk AI system [Art. 22(3)(d)].
* The representative must also be empowered to be addressed by authorities, either along with or instead of the provider, on all issues concerning compliance [Art. 22(3)].
* If the representative has reason to believe the provider is violating the regulation, it must end the mandate and immediately notify the market surveillance authority [Art. 22(4)].

For the purposes of this Regulation, the mandate shall empower the authorised representative to carry out the following tasks:
(d) cooperate with competent authorities, upon a reasoned request, in any action the latter take in relation to the high-risk AI system, in particular to reduce and mitigate the risks posed by the high-risk AI system;

question: Do providers of open-source general-purpose AI models need to appoint an authorised representative?
standalone_question: Do providers of open-source general-purpose AI models need to appoint an authorised representative under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Generally, no, providers of qualifying open-source general-purpose AI models do not need to appoint an authorised representative [Art. 54(6)]. However, they must still appoint one if the model presents systemic risks [Art. 54(6)].

Here are the key rules:
* While providers outside the EU must normally appoint an authorised representative in the Union before selling or offering a general-purpose AI model there [Art. 54(1)], an exception applies to open-source models [Art. 54(6)].
* An authorised representative is a person or company in the EU given a written mandate to act on the provider's behalf [Art. 3(5)].
* To qualify for the exemption, the model must be released under a free and open-source licence that permits access, usage, modification, and distribution [Art. 54(6)].
* Additionally, its parameters—including weights, architecture details, and usage information—must be publicly available, and the model must not present systemic risks [Art. 54(6)].

question: Are AI testing sandboxes supposed to help regulators in different countries work together?
standalone_question: Are AI regulatory sandboxes supposed to help regulators in different countries work together under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Yes, AI regulatory sandboxes are specifically meant to facilitate cross-border cooperation between authorities in different EU countries [Art. 57(13)]. 

Here are the key details from the Act:

* Sandboxes must be designed and run so that, where relevant, they help national competent authorities cooperate across borders [Art. 57(13)].
* Authorities can establish sandboxes jointly with the authorities of other Member States [Art. 57(2)].
* National authorities must inform the AI Office and the European Artificial Intelligence Board when they set up a sandbox, and they can request support and guidance [Art. 57(15)].
* The AI Office will publish and update a public list of planned and existing sandboxes specifically to encourage more interaction and cross-border cooperation [Art. 57(15)].

question: Where does a conformity assessment body send its application to become notified?
standalone_question: Where does a conformity assessment body send its application to become notified under the EU Artificial Intelligence Act?
answer:
A conformity assessment body must submit its application for notification to the notifying authority of the EU Member State in which it is established [Art. 29(1)]. 

Key details regarding this application include:
- The application must describe the assessment activities, the modules, and the types of AI systems the body claims competence for [Art. 29(2)].
- It must include an accreditation certificate from a national accreditation body if one exists, or all necessary documentary evidence to prove compliance if it cannot provide one [Art. 29(2)], [Art. 29(3)].
- Any valid documents and certificates from existing designations under other EU harmonisation laws may be included to support the application [Art. 29(2)], [Art. 29(4)].

question: Does a notified body get a separate ID number for each EU law it covers?
standalone_question: Does a notified body get a separate ID number for each EU law it covers under the EU AI Act?
answer:
No, a notified body does not receive a separate identification number for each EU law [Art. 35(1)].

* The Commission publishes and updates an official list of notified bodies, showing their single identification numbers and the activities they are approved to handle [Art. 35(2)].

question: What do I need to include in my technical documentation regarding standards if I haven't used any official EU harmonised ones?
standalone_question: What do I need to include in my technical documentation regarding standards if I haven't used any official EU harmonised ones under the AI Act?
answer:
If you have not applied official EU harmonised standards, you must provide a detailed description of the solutions you used to meet the legal requirements [Annex IV, point 7]. 

Here is what you must include in your technical documentation:
* A detailed description of the solutions adopted to meet the high-risk AI requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 [Annex IV, point 7].
* A list of any other relevant standards and technical specifications that you applied instead [Annex IV, point 7].
* Information demonstrating that your system complies with the necessary requirements, prepared before you sell or use the system and kept up to date [Art. 11(1)].
* If you are a small or medium-sized enterprise, including a start-up, you may choose to provide these required details in a simplified manner using a form established by the Commission [Art. 11(1)].

question: Under Article 46(3), what is needed to get an authorisation and who has to be told about it?
standalone_question: Under Article 46(3) of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, what is needed to get an authorisation and who has to be told about it?
answer:
Under Article 46(3), an authorisation can only be issued if the market surveillance authority concludes that the high-risk AI system complies with specific legal requirements, and both the Commission and other Member States must be informed [Art. 46(3)]. 

Here are the key details:
* The market surveillance authority must conclude that the high-risk AI system (an AI system presenting significant risks) complies with the requirements of Section 2 [Art. 46(3)].
* The market surveillance authority must inform the Commission of any authorisation it issues [Art. 46(3)].
* The authority must also inform the other Member States about the authorisation [Art. 46(3)].
* This notification requirement does not cover sensitive operational data relating to the activities of law-enforcement authorities [Art. 46(3)].

question: What can authorities do to stop a risky AI product from being sold?
standalone_question: What powers do market surveillance authorities have to stop a risky AI product from being made available on the market under the EU AI Act?
answer:
Market surveillance authorities have the power to restrict, prohibit, withdraw, or recall risky or non-compliant AI systems from the market [Art. 79(5)], [Art. 83(2)]. 

Key powers include:
* Prohibiting or restricting an AI system from being sold or used, or withdrawing or recalling it, if the operator fails to take adequate corrective action in time [Art. 79(5)].
* Taking prompt, appropriate restrictive measures, including withdrawing the AI product or system from their national market [Art. 79(9)].
* Restricting or banning high-risk AI systems (systems that carry significant risks) or ensuring they are recalled or withdrawn without delay if formal non-compliance persists [Art. 83(2)].
* Requesting access to the source code of a high-risk AI system to check conformity, provided this is necessary and other testing, auditing, or documentation checks have been exhausted or proved insufficient [Art. 74(13)].

question: What should a high-risk AI's logging feature be able to record?
standalone_question: What should a high-risk AI system's logging feature be able to record under the EU AI Act?
answer:
A high-risk AI system—meaning an AI system subject to strict regulatory requirements—must technically allow for the automatic recording of events, known as logs, throughout its entire lifetime [Art. 12(1)]. The system must record events that help trace how it works based on its intended purpose [Art. 12(2)].

Specifically, the logging capabilities must record:

* Events relevant for spotting situations where the system may present a risk or undergo a substantial change [Art. 12(2)(a)].
* Events relevant for facilitating post-market monitoring and monitoring the ongoing operation of the system [Art. 12(2)(b)], [Art. 12(2)(c)].
* For certain specific systems (referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III), at a minimum: the start and end date and time of each use [Art. 12(3)(a)].
* For those same specific systems, at a minimum: the reference database used, the input data that resulted in a match, and the identity of the people who verified the results [Art. 12(3)(b)], [Art. 12(3)(c)], [Art. 12(3)(d)].

(b) facilitating the post-market monitoring referred to in Article 72; and
(c) monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5).

question: Who is responsible for creating a way to assess AI risk levels when updating the lists of banned or regulated systems?

answer:
The AI Office is responsible for developing this methodology [Art. 112(11)]. 

* The AI Office must develop an objective and participative method to evaluate risk levels, which means looking at the likelihood and severity of harm [Art. 112(11)], [Art. 3(2)].
* This method is used to guide evaluations and reviews regarding adding new systems to the list of banned practices in Article 5 [Art. 112(11)].
* It also guides adding systems or new area headings to the list of high-risk AI systems in Annex III [Art. 112(11)].
* Additionally, the methodology guides adding systems to the list of those requiring extra transparency measures under Article 50 [Art. 112(11)].

To guide the evaluations and reviews referred to in paragraphs 1 to 7 of this Article, the AI Office shall undertake to develop an objective and participative methodology for the evaluation of risk levels based on the criteria outlined in the relevant Articles and the inclusion of new systems in:
(a) the list set out in Annex III, including the extension of existing area headings or the addition of new area headings in that Annex;
(b) the list of prohibited practices set out in Article 5; and

question: What happens if a company doesn't fix a risky AI system in time?
